Dizu Plaatjies [6162]

By: Marion Edmunds | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The Man behind the Marimbas - a profile piece about Dizu Plaatjies, teacher of indigenous music

Unique Selling Point:
Dizu Plaatjies is a giant in South African traditional music. He grew up the son of a Sangoma in Pondoland, and learned traditional ways and music at his knee. As a young man he mastered the marimbas through a church band and then developed a style of using marimbas and traditional instruments to play indigenous music, forming the band Amanpondo which toured the world during apartheid, bringing indigenous sounds and African music and melodies to European audiences. Since then, he has developed as a teacher and maker of indigenous instruments, and has been promoted to a Professor at the University of Cape Town where he manages a course in traditional musical performance, and hands his skills down to students in the Music Faculty.


Summary:
One of his most promising students, Zinzi Najova, is now starting to make her names as a traditional performer, in particular of the uHadi, and ancient calabash and bow instrument which hails from the Eastern Cape and Kwazulu-Natal. It is traditionally played by older women, and Dizu has promoted older players from the rural areas, and then passed the gift of playing down to women like Zinzi, who is grew up in an urban environment but still reaches out to past traditional sounds and customs.

Dizu still tours globally in university holidays with a traditional band called the Ibuyembo Ensemble and teaches at schools, using a collection of traditional instruments he has at his home in Langa.

We will film Dizu showing us his instruments and telling us his story, with some use of archive, which is limited. And we will interview Zinzi Najova briefly about her journey and what Dizu has taught us and why that is important to young people, even in an urban setting. The filming will take place in Langa, at Dizu's house with a drone shot of the environment.

Script:


DIZU PLAATJIES

DRONE SHOT OF LANGA – sound of music of Dizu playing the bow

Dizu Plaatjies:
I always say that our fathers and mothers created this beautiful instrument, and they left it for us to continue. But now, because of we are so Western minded, and because of the places that where we are living, it's so modern and we tend to ignore where we come from. And we ignore what we used to play in the olden days.

Sequence of Dizu and Claire walking in Langa

(VO)
DIZU PLAATJIES IS A MULTI-AWARD-WINNING MUSICIAN, GROUNDED IN THE ANCIENT TRADITIONS OF AFRICA.
BORN IN RURAL TRANSKEI, DIZU CAME TO THE CITY AS A YOUNG BOY.
BUT EVEN IN A TOWNSHIP, HE WAS SUSTAINED BY HIS XHOSA HERITAGE.

Dizu Plaatjies:
My father is a traditional healer, eh, we have all these diviner ceremonies that are taking place in our during weekends, which now it was a lesson for all the family to be part and parcel, so that we've got to witness what my father was doing.

Claire: I don't know the name of any of these instruments. Can you tell me what is this that you have in your hand?

Dizu: Okay, this one is called uHadi. This is the main major instrument of the Xhosa speaking people, but I'm saying Nguni, but it is an instrument that is performed in play by women at night.

Dizu: What you do, you take your three fingers to hold the stick and the seven is outside, then you just do like that. Like that, and then like that. So now here, I'll be opening and closing even go down line (he plays)

(VO)
WITH A NATURAL TALENT FOR PERFORMANCE, DIZU ALSO LEARNT TO PLAY THE MARIMBAS AT CHURCH. HE THEN DID WHAT ENERGETIC YOUNG MUSICIANS DO THE WORLD OVER – HE FORMED A BAND. IT WAS THE START OF AN INCREDIBLE JOURNEY, DESPITE THE SHACKLES OF APARTHEID.

Claire Mawisa:
A journey that would end up with Dizu being celebrated on international stages all started here in Langa with his marimba band Amampondo, busking illegally on the streets of Cape Town.

Dizu Plaatjies:
I was the first to take them out of South Africa, out of the church straight, you know, to the international stages. Across the world today, people are playing marimba, even though there were countries that had their own marimbas, and so on, but they've never made marimba famous, like I did with Amampondo.

(VO)
AMAMPONDO BECAME A HOUSEHOLD NAME IN SOUTH AFRICA IN THE 1980’S – THEY BURST ON TO THE MUSICAL SCENE LOCALLY, AND THEN TRAVELLED THE WORLD, PIONEERING INDIGENOUS PERFORMANCE, TAKING THE SOUNDS OF SOUTH AFRICA TO ALL FOUR CORNERS OF THE GLOBE.

Dizu Plaatjies:
We're unstoppable. Since since we started travelling, Eastern and Western Europe, Asia, North America, South America, Madagascar, Australia, all the continents and Soviet Union. I know all the continents of the globe. I've travelled almost about 90 different countries, I have 12 Passports

Sequence: Dizu goes into his storeroom/workshop fiddles with bits and pieces – breather but should take care of voice over below

(VO)
AS HE GREW AS A PERFORMER, SO DID DIZU’S INTEREST IN TRADITIONAL INSTRUMENTS. HE SOUGHT OUT THEIR ORIGINS, STUDIED THEIR DESIGN AND LEARNT TO PLAY THEM. HE SET UP HIS OWN WORKSHOP, SO HE COULD MAKE MORE AND SHARE HIS KNOWLEDGE.

Dizu: This one is called is called a rainstick. You know, even now even though it's not raining, but these are the kinds of sounds that you get....while I'm playing the other instruments to do that and go back into that into that. And then when they seeds are finishing, then you turn it again.

Hands it to Claire – close ups of her turning the rain stick - czn cut byte below over it
Dizu Plaatjies:
I never wanted to limit myself with instrument because we Xhosa people, we've got only four different instruments. I wanted to have more. When I look at the size of Africa, I said, if there are more than 1500 languages that are spoken in Africa, what about instruments?

Claire Mawisa:
Each of these traditional instruments don't just make a sound. They tell an intimate story of a culture that's fast disappearing.

Claire: This is the Calabash?
Dizu: You've got to cut in a way because this one as you can see, it's a it's an old calabash for old women. But now that this part, they always have to measure their breasts before cutting the ca;abash. Oh, because this course is got to go to the breasts of a woman and then the sound becomes so beautiful.


Dizu Plaatjies:
Now, the task was me and the children, as I'm saying, said to you that my mother was a teacher. So teaching, I started teaching my own family.

(VO)
DIZU’S NEICE, THABISA DINGA, LEARNT AT HER UNCLE’S KNEE, AND BY FIFTEEN SHE WAS A PERFORMER IN HER OWN RIGHT.
Sequence: Dizu playing with his niece Thabiso Dinga

Thabisa Dinga:
0:46 I first encountered African indigenous instruments here. When I got in Cape Town, when I came to live with my uncle, we would have tourists coming over the house. And my uncle, tell me Okay, now, next time the tourists are coming, now you have to play for them. I'm not gonna be there sometimes. So you have to take over.

Claire looking at Thabiso’s phone with her – some archive shots
Sound up:
Thabisa says:In Malaysia, at the Womad Festival…

(VO)
OF ALL THE INSTRUMENTS, THABISA HAS THIS FAVOURITE.

Thabisa Dinga:
It was the Mbira Dzvadzimo. That is the instrument. It's called the thumb piano with English. And it is made out of metal notes that you strike with your fingers. And yes, it has a Calabash around it. So it's called spirits of Mbira Dzvadzimo the notes of the ancestral spirits, it's from Zimbabwe.

Claire Mawisa:
Hailed as an international superstar, Dizu never abandoned his roots. He shifted his focus and started teaching the next generation and became a professor at the University of Cape Town.

(VO)
DIZU HOPES TO INSPIRE HIS YOUNG PROTEGEES TO TAKE INDIGENOUS INSTRUMENTS OFF THE SHELF AND ONTO THE STAGE, SO THAT THEY BECOME ONCE AGAIN PART OF CONTEMPORARY CULTURE.

Dizu Plaatjies: Oh, so each and every student that I've taught, especially once I saw a person on stage, I feel so happy, because now I can see, you know, the seeds that I plough, you know, I can look at this person that said that, at least what I've implemented to her, it will never die. You know, because I'm trying to, you know, to treasure this instrument not to die, you know. So now, I've got to share, with other people, and they've got to do the same thing.

(VO)
THABISA IS OFTEN ON STAGE WITH HER UNCLE; SHE’S AN IMPORTANT MEMBER OF HIS GROUP, IBUYAMBO, A MODERN MUSICAL COLLECTIVE EVOKING THE ANCIENT SOUNDS OF AFRICA, BRINGING THE PAST TO THE PRESENT MOMENT.

Thabisa Dinga:
These instruments are very, I would say they're very sacred. And they actually do carry a lot, a lot of history. And I feel that it's the only way that we can preserve our culture and pass it on to the next generation is by keep on playing these instruments. They should not die at any given point. It is our identity, it is who we are. So it is very important for us to preserve and pass it on.
